explanation: silvā is ablative singular because it follows in and ends in long -ā; with in plus the ablative it tells where something is.
via has a short final -a, so it is nominative singular, and est needs a subject; via is the only word that can be it.
sunt is plural and needs a plural subject; Amīcī is the only candidate, so it is nominative plural rather than genitive singular.
The ending -ōrum is only genitive plural; fīliōrum tells whose friends they are.
agrīs could be dative or ablative plural by form, but it follows in, which takes the ablative to show where the friends are.
castra is a plural-only neuter noun; after in, the -īs ending is ablative plural telling where the dangers are.
perīcula could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but sunt takes no object and needs a plural subject, so it is nominative.
bellī is genitive singular (of war) describing perīcula; a neuter nominative plural would be bella, not bellī.
Mīlitēs could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but sunt has no object and needs a plural subject, so it is nominative.
The ending -is on rēx is only genitive singular; rēgis tells whose camp it is.
Pāx is nominative singular and comes first, so it is the subject of est; salūs then renames it.
salūs is nominative singular after the linking verb est and renames the subject Pāx, so it is a predicate nominative.
Corpora could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but sunt takes no object and needs a plural subject, so it is nominative.
The ending -e on flūmen is ablative singular, and it follows in, which with the ablative tells where the bodies are.
Urbs is nominative singular and comes first, so it is the subject that est links to caput.
caput looks the same in nominative and accusative, but est is a linking verb and takes no object; caput renames the subject Urbs, so it is a predicate nominative.
The ending -is on gēns is only genitive singular; gentis tells whose head the city is.
Adventus has a short -us, so it is nominative singular (the genitive would be adventūs with a long ū); it is the subject of est.
The long -ūs could be genitive singular or nominative/accusative plural, but est is singular and takes no object, so exercitūs must be genitive telling whose arrival it is.
Spēs could be nominative singular or accusative plural by form, but est is singular and takes no object, so Spēs is its singular subject.
The ending -e on virtūs is ablative singular, and after in it tells where the hope lies.
Nautae could be genitive, dative, or nominative plural by form, but servant is plural and needs a plural subject, and nauta is masculine even though it looks first declension.
The ending -ās is only accusative plural; portās receives the action of servant.
servant has the present stem servā- plus the ending -nt, which is third person plural; it states a fact, so it is indicative.
The ending -um is accusative singular; Chrīstum receives the action of laudāmus, whose subject is we.
The ending -mus means we, first person plural; the present stem laudā- with no tense sign makes it present, and it states a fact.
The long -ā marks ablative singular, and after in it tells where the roads are being prepared.
The ending -tis means you (plural), second person plural; parā- with no tense sign is present, and the sentence states a fact.

sentence: Rēgem nōn timeō, sed Deum timeō.
explanation: The ending -em is accusative singular; Rēgem is what is not feared, the object of timeō.

sentence: Rēgem nōn timeō, sed Deum timeō.
explanation: The ending -ō means I, first person singular; the present stem timē- with no tense sign makes it present indicative.
The ending -em is accusative singular; legiōnem is what the leader leads, while Dux is already the nominative subject.
flūmen looks the same in nominative and accusative, but it follows ad, which always takes the accusative; with the verb of motion dūcit, ad flūmen names the place the legion is led to.
The ending -t is third person singular, agreeing with Dux; the vowel -i- before it marks the third-conjugation present (the future would be dūcet).

sentence: Gallī oppida capiunt et agrōs vāstant.
explanation: oppida could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but Gallī is already the subject of capiunt, so oppida is what they capture.

sentence: Gallī oppida capiunt et agrōs vāstant.
explanation: The ending -unt is third person plural, agreeing with Gallī; -iunt on capiō marks the present of a third-conjugation -iō verb.

sentence: Signum audītis et in castra venītis.
explanation: The ending -tis means you (plural); audī- with no tense sign is present, and it states a fact.

sentence: Signum audītis et in castra venītis.
explanation: castra is a plural-only neuter noun; with the verb of motion venītis, in plus the accusative means into the camp, the place you come to.
Gallīs could be dative or ablative plural by form, but the preposition cum takes the ablative and tells with whom the Romans fought.
The tense sign -bā- marks the imperfect, and -nt is third person plural agreeing with Rōmānī; saepe (often) fits the repeated past action.
erat is the imperfect of sum, third person singular, agreeing with Rōma; it describes a past state.
caput looks the same in nominative and accusative, but erat is a linking verb with no object; caput renames the subject Rōma.
Exercitus has a short -us, so it is nominative singular (not genitive or plural, which would be exercitūs); noster agrees with it and superābit is singular.
hostēs could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but the verb is singular and Exercitus is already its subject, so hostēs is what the army will overcome.
The tense sign -bi- marks the future in the first conjugation, and -t is third person singular agreeing with Exercitus.
The ending -e on urbs is ablative singular, and after in it tells where we will stay.
The tense sign -bi- marks the future in the second conjugation, and -mus means we, first person plural.
Nautīs could be dative or ablative plural by form, but with the verb of giving dabis it names the people to whom grain is given; there is no preposition to make it ablative.
The tense sign -bi- marks the future, and the ending -s means you (singular), second person singular.

sentence: Caesar in Galliam vēnit et Gallōs vīcit.
explanation: The ending -am is accusative singular, and with the verb of motion vēnit, in plus the accusative means into Gaul, the place Caesar came to.

sentence: Caesar in Galliam vēnit et Gallōs vīcit.
explanation: The long ē shows the perfect stem vēn- (the present is venit with a short e); -it is third person singular agreeing with Caesar.
hominibus could be dative or ablative plural by form, but with the verb of giving dedit it names the people to whom the law was given, and there is no preposition.
dedit is built on the perfect stem ded- of dō, with the perfect ending -it, third person singular agreeing with Deus.
The ending -em is accusative singular; Frātrem is the person you saw, the object of vīdistī.
vīd- is the perfect stem of videō, and the ending -istī is only perfect second person singular (you).
castra is a plural-only neuter noun that looks the same in nominative and accusative, but Gallī is already the subject of mūnīverant, so castra is what they had fortified.
The perfect stem mūnīv- plus -erant marks the pluperfect (had fortified), third person plural agreeing with Gallī; iam (already) fits the earlier past time.
The perfect stem vīc- plus -eritis (with a short i) marks the future perfect, second person plural; in a sī clause with a future main verb it is indicative, not subjunctive.
The tense sign -bi- marks the future in the second conjugation, and -tis means you (plural), second person plural.

sentence: Tempore bellī frūmentum in castra portāverō.
explanation: The ending -e on tempus is ablative singular, and a time word in the ablative without a preposition tells when the action happens.

sentence: Tempore bellī frūmentum in castra portāverō.
explanation: The perfect stem portāv- plus -erō marks the future perfect, first person singular (I will have carried); the perfect itself would be portāvī.
mīlitibus could be dative or ablative plural by form, but ā plus the ablative with a passive verb names the people by whom the city is defended.
The ending -tur is the passive third person singular; the vowel -i- before it marks the third-conjugation present, and Urbs is the subject being defended.
Gallīs follows ā and goes with a passive verb, so it is ablative plural naming the people by whom we were attacked.
The tense sign -bā- marks the imperfect, and the ending -mur is the passive form of -mus, first person plural (we were being attacked).

sentence: Frūmentum in castra ā servīs portābitur.
explanation: Frūmentum looks the same in nominative and accusative, but portābitur is passive and takes no object, so Frūmentum is its subject.

sentence: Frūmentum in castra ā servīs portābitur.
explanation: The tense sign -bi- marks the future, and -tur is the passive third person singular ending agreeing with Frūmentum.
Rōmānīs follows ā and goes with the passive victī sunt, so it is ablative plural naming the people by whom the Gauls were conquered.
The perfect passive is two words: the participle victī (masculine plural, agreeing with Gallī) plus sunt, the present of sum, which together mean were conquered.
Oppidum looks the same in nominative and accusative, but captum erat is passive and takes no object, so Oppidum is the subject that was captured.
The participle captum (neuter singular, agreeing with Oppidum) plus erat, the imperfect of sum, forms the pluperfect passive: had been captured.
hostēs could be nominative or accusative plural by form, but potest is singular and Dux is its subject, so hostēs is the object of the infinitive superāre.
potest is the present of possum, third person singular agreeing with Dux; it is completed by the infinitive superāre.
pugnant is the main verb stating what the soldiers do; the ending -nt is third person plural agreeing with Mīlitēs, and pugnā- with no tense sign is present.
servent has the vowel -e- instead of -a- in a first-conjugation verb, the sign of the present subjunctive; ut after a verb of action tells why they fight, so the clause is purpose.

sentence: Ad urbem veniō ut mātrem videam.
explanation: The ending -em is accusative singular; mātrem is the person I want to see, the object of videam.

sentence: Ad urbem veniō ut mātrem videam.
explanation: videam has -a- added to the second-conjugation stem, the sign of the present subjunctive, and -m means I; ut after veniō explains the reason for coming, so it is a purpose clause.

sentence: Mīlitēs, in castrīs manētis nē ab hostibus capiāminī.
explanation: Mīlitēs is set off by a comma and the verb manētis is second person (you), so the soldiers are being spoken to; that makes it vocative, not nominative or accusative.

sentence: Mīlitēs, in castrīs manētis nē ab hostibus capiāminī.
explanation: capiāminī has the subjunctive vowel -ā- and the passive ending -minī (you, plural); nē introduces a negative purpose clause telling why you stay in camp.

sentence: Dux mīlitēs mīsit ut castra mūnīrent.
explanation: mīs- is the perfect stem of mittō, and -it is third person singular agreeing with Dux; it is the main verb stating what the leader did.

sentence: Dux mīlitēs mīsit ut castra mūnīrent.
explanation: mūnīrent is the infinitive mūnīre plus -nt, the form of the imperfect subjunctive; it follows the past main verb mīsit, and ut tells why the soldiers were sent, so it is purpose.

sentence: In silvam vēnistī ut hostēs vidērēs.
explanation: The ending -am is accusative singular, and with the verb of motion vēnistī, in plus the accusative means into the forest, the place you came to.

sentence: In silvam vēnistī ut hostēs vidērēs.
explanation: vidērēs is the infinitive vidēre plus -s (you), the imperfect subjunctive after the past verb vēnistī; ut explains why you came, so the clause is purpose.

sentence: Tanta erat virtūs mīlitum ut hostēs nōn pugnārent.
explanation: virtūs is nominative singular, the subject of erat; the adjective Tanta agrees with it and describes it.

sentence: Tanta erat virtūs mīlitum ut hostēs nōn pugnārent.
explanation: pugnārent is the infinitive pugnāre plus -nt, the imperfect subjunctive; the word tanta (so great) in the main clause signals that ut introduces a result, and the negative is nōn, not nē.

sentence: Rēx tam malus est ut populus eum timeat.
explanation: populus is nominative singular, the subject of timeat inside the ut clause; eum is the object.

sentence: Rēx tam malus est ut populus eum timeat.
explanation: timeat has -a- added to the second-conjugation stem, the sign of the present subjunctive, with -t agreeing with populus; tam (so) in the main clause marks the ut clause as result.

sentence: Dux mīlitēs monuit ut castra dēfenderent.
explanation: monu- is the perfect stem of moneō, and -it is third person singular agreeing with Dux; it is the main verb.

sentence: Dux mīlitēs monuit ut castra dēfenderent.
explanation: dēfenderent is the infinitive dēfendere plus -nt, the imperfect subjunctive after past monuit; because moneō is a verb of advising, the ut clause gives the content of the advice (to defend the camp), an indirect command.

sentence: Marīam ōrāmus ut prō nōbīs ōret.
explanation: The ending -am is accusative singular; Marīam is the person we pray to, the object of ōrāmus.

sentence: Marīam ōrāmus ut prō nōbīs ōret.
explanation: ōret has -e- instead of -a- in a first-conjugation verb, the sign of the present subjunctive; because ōrāmus is a verb of asking, the ut clause tells what we ask her to do, an indirect command.

sentence: Cum Caesar in Galliam vēnisset, Gallī pācem petīvērunt.
explanation: vēnisset is the perfect stem vēn- plus -isset, the pluperfect subjunctive, third person singular agreeing with Caesar; cum with the subjunctive here simply gives the circumstances (when Caesar had come) under which the Gauls acted.

sentence: Cum Caesar in Galliam vēnisset, Gallī pācem petīvērunt.
explanation: petīv- is the perfect stem of petō, and -ērunt is the perfect third person plural ending agreeing with Gallī; this is the main verb of the sentence.

sentence: Cum ducem nōn habērent, mīlitēs ex urbe nōn vēnērunt.
explanation: The ending -em is accusative singular; ducem is what the soldiers did not have, the object of habērent.

sentence: Cum ducem nōn habērent, mīlitēs ex urbe nōn vēnērunt.
explanation: habērent is the infinitive habēre plus -nt, the imperfect subjunctive; the cum clause gives the reason the soldiers did not come out (since they had no leader), so it is causal.

sentence: Cum urbs magna esset, hostēs tamen eam cēpērunt.
explanation: esset is the imperfect subjunctive of sum, third person singular agreeing with urbs; tamen (nevertheless) in the main clause shows the cum clause states something true in spite of which the enemy acted, so it is concessive.

sentence: Cum urbs magna esset, hostēs tamen eam cēpērunt.
explanation: cēp- is the perfect stem of capiō, and -ērunt is the perfect third person plural ending agreeing with hostēs; it is the main verb of the sentence.
Servāte is the present stem servā- plus -te, the plural command ending; the exclamation point and the vocative mīlitēs show that soldiers are being ordered.
mīlitēs is set off by a comma after a command, so the soldiers are being addressed; the command already has its object urbem, so mīlitēs is vocative.
Ōrā is the bare present stem with a long -ā and no personal ending, which is the singular command form; it is addressed to Marīa.
Marīa has a short final -a and is set off by a comma after the command Ōrā, so Mary is the person being spoken to; the ablative would be Marīā with a long ā.
audit is the present of audiō, third person singular agreeing with Imperātor; the short -i- before -t marks the present (the future would be audiet).
timeant has -a- added to the second-conjugation stem, the sign of the present subjunctive; the question word cūr after the verb audit shows this is a question reported indirectly.

sentence: Dux rogat ubi hostēs castra posuerint.
explanation: rogat is the present of rogō, third person singular agreeing with Dux; it is the main verb that introduces the question.

sentence: Dux rogat ubi hostēs castra posuerint.
explanation: posuerint is the perfect stem posu- plus -erint; this form could also be future perfect indicative, but the question word ubi after rogat makes it an indirect question, which takes the subjunctive, so it is perfect subjunctive.
audīv- is the perfect stem of audiō, and -imus means we, first person plural; it is the main verb stating what we heard.
rēx is nominative singular, the subject of dīxisset inside the question clause; quid is the thing he said.
dīxisset is the perfect stem dīx- plus -isset, the pluperfect subjunctive, third person singular agreeing with rēx; the question word quid after Audīvimus marks an indirect question.
